slides.narration: Pump up a tyre and it feels firm. Leave a closed bottle in the sun and it bulges. Both are the work of gas molecules, which never stop moving. This part explains why, and ends with the first gas law.

slides.heading: Molecules of a gas in motion

rows: Molecules are far apart and free to move anywhere in the container

visual.alt: Table of properties of gases and the molecular explanation

slides.narration: In a gas the molecules are far apart and move at random in straight lines, bouncing off each other and off the walls. That is why a gas has no fixed shape, fills its container and can be squeezed into a smaller space.

slides.heading: What is gas pressure?
slides.body_md: The **pressure** of a gas is the force its molecules exert on each unit area of the container wall. It is caused by their **constant collisions** with the wall.

nodes.label: A tiny push on the wall

visual.alt: Flow: a molecule hits the wall, a tiny push, billions of hits, steady pressure

slides.narration: Each molecule that strikes the wall gives it a tiny push. There are so many collisions every second that the pushes blend into one steady force on each unit of area. That steady push is the pressure of the gas.

slides.heading: Quick check: the cause of pressure
slides.body_md: A gas in a sealed flask presses on the walls because its molecules…
slides.narration: Think about what the molecules are doing all the time.

slides.heading: Heating a gas

rows: Gas in a closed rigid vessel is heated
Molecules move faster, so they hit the wall harder and more often
Gas under a free-moving piston is heated
Faster molecules push the piston up until the hits per unit area are back to the outside pressure
Slower molecules hit the wall less hard and less often

visual.alt: Table of the effect of heating and cooling a gas explained by molecular motion

slides.narration: Heat makes the molecules move faster. In a rigid closed vessel they hit the walls harder and more often, so the pressure rises. Under a free piston the faster molecules push it up, so the volume grows. Cooling does the opposite.

slides.heading: Boyle's law
slides.body_md: **Boyle's law:** at constant temperature, the volume of a fixed mass of gas is **inversely proportional** to its pressure.
slides.narration: Boyle's law says that if you keep the temperature and the amount of gas fixed, then doubling the pressure halves the volume. The product of pressure and volume stays the same. So the first pressure times the first volume equals the second pressure times the second volume.

slides.heading: Testing Boyle's law
slides.body_md: Load on the piston is changed; the bath keeps the temperature steady; pressure and volume are noted each time.

slides.heading: Readings from an experiment
slides.body_md: Imagined readings for a trapped gas at constant temperature. The last column is the product P × V.

visual.alt: Table of five volume and pressure readings with their products all equal to twelve thousand

slides.narration: As the volume falls, the pressure rises. Multiply each pair of readings and the product is always the same, twelve thousand. That constant product is the evidence for Boyle's law.

slides.heading: Quick check: reading a table
slides.body_md: In a Boyle experiment the readings are 30 cm³ at 400 mm Hg and 60 cm³ at an unknown pressure. What is the unknown pressure?
slides.narration: The product of pressure and volume must stay the same.

slides.heading: Graph of P against V
slides.body_md: A fixed mass of gas at constant temperature gives a **curve** that falls as V rises and never meets either axis.

visual.alt: Graph of pressure against volume at constant temperature: a falling curve through the points twenty and six hundred, forty and three hundred, one hundred and one hundred and twenty, that never touches either axis
visual.caption: Boyle experiment readings (imagined). P against V is a curve (a rectangular hyperbola).

slides.narration: Plot pressure on the vertical axis and volume on the horizontal axis. The points fall on a smooth curve that drops steeply at first and then flattens. It never touches either axis, because the volume cannot be zero and the pressure cannot be zero.

slides.heading: Graph of P against 1/V
slides.body_md: Plotting pressure against the **reciprocal of the volume** turns the curve into a **straight line through the origin**.

visual.alt: Graph of pressure against the reciprocal of volume: the same five readings fall on a straight line that passes through the origin
visual.caption: The same readings plotted as P against 1/V (here 100 divided by V). The straight line through the origin shows that P is proportional to 1/V.

slides.narration: Now plot pressure against one divided by the volume. The five points fall on a straight line that passes through the origin. A straight line through the origin means the two quantities are directly proportional, so pressure is proportional to one over the volume.

slides.heading: Quick check: which graph?
slides.body_md: Which graph for a fixed mass of gas at constant temperature is a straight line through the origin?
slides.narration: Remember that the straight line comes from the reciprocal of the volume.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: a bicycle pump
slides.body_md: A pump holds 400 cm³ of air at 760 mm Hg. The outlet is blocked and the air is pushed into 100 cm³ with the temperature unchanged. Find the final pressure.
bullets: Step 1: P₁ = 760 mm Hg, V₁ = 400 cm³, V₂ = 100 cm³, P₂ = ?
Step 2: write P₁V₁ = P₂V₂, so P₂ = P₁V₁ ÷ V₂.
Check: the volume fell to a quarter, so the pressure rose four-fold.

visual.alt: Worked table for the pump

slides.narration: Write down what is given, then use the Boyle's law equation. Seven hundred and sixty times four hundred divided by one hundred gives three thousand forty millimetres of mercury. The volume fell to a quarter, so the pressure became four times larger. That makes sense.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: nitrogen expands
slides.body_md: 750 cm³ of nitrogen at 600 mm Hg expands at constant temperature until the pressure is 450 mm Hg. Find the new volume.
bullets: Step 2: V₂ = P₁V₁ ÷ P₂.
Check: the pressure fell, so the volume must rise. It did.

visual.alt: Worked table: pressure falls and volume rises

slides.narration: This time the pressure falls, so the volume must rise. Six hundred times seven hundred and fifty divided by four hundred and fifty gives one thousand cubic centimetres. Always check that your answer moves in the right direction.

slides.heading: Quick check: compressing hydrogen
slides.body_md: 900 cm³ of hydrogen at 760 mm Hg is compressed at constant temperature to one third of its volume. Find the final pressure in mm Hg.
slides.narration: If the volume falls to one third, what happens to the pressure?

slides.heading: Summary
bullets: A gas exerts pressure because its molecules keep hitting the walls.
Heating makes molecules faster: pressure rises in a closed vessel, volume rises under a free piston.
Boyle's law: at constant temperature P × V is constant for a fixed mass of gas.
P against V is a curve; P against 1/V is a straight line through the origin.

visual.alt: Summary table of Boyle's law

slides.narration: To recap. Gas pressure comes from molecular collisions. Heating speeds the molecules up. Boyle's law says that at constant temperature the product of pressure and volume is constant, so one equation links the first and second states. The graph of pressure against reciprocal volume is a straight line through the origin.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: State **constant temperature** and **fixed mass** in Boyle's law.
Use the same units for both volumes and both pressures.
Give the graph shapes: a **curve** for P against V; a **straight line through the origin** for P against 1/V.
Explain with molecules: smaller volume means **more collisions per unit area**.
slides.narration: Exam tips. When you state Boyle's law, say constant temperature and fixed mass. Keep the units the same on both sides. Describe the graph shapes correctly. And explain pressure changes with molecules: a smaller space means more collisions on each unit of wall area.

slides.heading: Charles's Law and the Gas Equation
slides.body_md: Part 2 — what heating does to the volume of a gas, the coldest possible temperature, and one equation for everything.

visual.alt: Flow: temperature scales, Charles's law, gas equation and STP

slides.narration: A balloon left in a warm car swells; in a freezer it shrinks. Part two studies this effect, finds the lowest temperature anything can reach, and joins the two gas laws into a single equation.

slides.heading: Heating a gas at constant pressure
slides.body_md: When a fixed mass of gas is heated under a **free piston**, the pressure stays at the outside value. The faster molecules push the piston up and the **volume rises**; on cooling it **falls**.

visual.alt: Flow: heating, faster molecules, piston pushed up, volume increases

slides.narration: Heat the gas and the molecules speed up. They push harder on the piston, which rises until the push per unit area balances the outside air again. The pressure is the same as before, but the volume is larger.

slides.heading: Celsius and kelvin scales
slides.body_md: The **kelvin** (absolute) scale starts at the lowest possible temperature, **0 K**. A kelvin degree is the same size as a Celsius degree.

slides.narration: The Celsius scale puts zero at the melting point of ice. The kelvin scale puts zero at absolute zero, which is two hundred and seventy three degrees below that. To change Celsius to kelvin, add two hundred and seventy three.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: changing scales
slides.body_md: Convert (i) 27 °C to kelvin, (ii) −73 °C to kelvin, (iii) 350 K to °C.
bullets: Step 1: kelvin = Celsius + 273.
(iii) Celsius = kelvin − 273 = 350 − 273 = **77 °C**.

visual.alt: Table of three conversions between degrees Celsius and kelvin

slides.narration: To go from Celsius to kelvin, add two hundred and seventy three. Twenty seven becomes three hundred. Minus seventy three becomes two hundred. To go back, subtract two hundred and seventy three, so three hundred and fifty kelvin is seventy seven degrees Celsius.

slides.heading: Quick check: a kelvin temperature
slides.body_md: What is 47 °C on the kelvin scale?
slides.narration: Add two hundred and seventy three.

slides.heading: Charles's law
slides.body_md: **Charles's law:** at constant pressure, the volume of a fixed mass of gas is **directly proportional to its absolute (kelvin) temperature**. Temperatures must be in kelvin.
slides.narration: Charles's law says that at constant pressure the volume of a fixed mass of gas is directly proportional to its temperature on the kelvin scale. Doubling the kelvin temperature doubles the volume. You must always change degrees Celsius to kelvin before using it.

slides.heading: Graph of V against Celsius temperature
slides.body_md: A straight line, but **not** through the origin. Extend it backwards (**extrapolate**): it reaches **zero volume at −273 °C**.

functions.label: Volume of the gas at constant pressure

visual.alt: Graph of volume against Celsius temperature at constant pressure: a straight line rising through four measured points; extended backwards it reaches zero volume at minus two hundred and seventy three degrees Celsius
visual.caption: Imagined readings at constant pressure. The line is extended (extrapolated) below the lowest reading.

slides.narration: The volume rises steadily with temperature, giving a straight line. Extend the line backwards beyond the lowest reading, and it meets the zero volume level at minus two hundred and seventy three degrees Celsius. This is a way of finding absolute zero from measurements.

slides.heading: Absolute zero
slides.body_md: On the kelvin scale the same line passes through the **origin**. **Absolute zero** is 0 K, or −273 °C, the lowest possible temperature. A real gas turns into a liquid before it gets there, so the line is an extrapolation.

visual.alt: Graph of volume against kelvin temperature at constant pressure: a straight line through the origin passing through the four points
visual.caption: The same readings on the kelvin scale: a straight line through the origin.

slides.narration: On the kelvin scale the same line passes through the origin, so volume is directly proportional to kelvin temperature. Absolute zero is zero kelvin. In practice, real gases liquefy before reaching it, so the zero volume point is found only by extending the line.

slides.heading: Quick check: the V–t line
slides.body_md: Extrapolating the straight-line graph of volume against Celsius temperature to zero volume gives a temperature of…
slides.narration: This is the temperature called absolute zero.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: Charles's law
slides.body_md: 580 cm³ of hydrogen at 17 °C is heated at constant pressure to 77 °C. Find the new volume.
bullets: Step 2: V₂ = V₁ × T₂ ÷ T₁.
Check: the gas was heated, so the volume rose.

visual.alt: Worked table for the Charles law example

slides.narration: First change both temperatures to kelvin, which gives two hundred and ninety and three hundred and fifty. Then multiply the volume by the ratio of the final to the initial temperature. Five hundred and eighty times three hundred and fifty divided by two hundred and ninety is seven hundred cubic centimetres.

slides.heading: The combined gas equation
slides.body_md: Change the pressure and the temperature together: first apply **Boyle's law** at the first temperature, then **Charles's law** at the final pressure.

nodes.label: Boyle at T₁: V₁ becomes V′ at P₂
Charles at P₂: V′ becomes V₂ at T₂

visual.alt: Flow showing the two steps that lead to the combined gas equation

slides.narration: Take a gas from the first state to the second in two steps. First change the pressure at the original temperature, using Boyle. Then change the temperature at the new pressure, using Charles. Putting the two steps together gives one equation: pressure times volume over temperature stays constant. Temperatures must be in kelvin.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: the combined equation
slides.body_md: 300 cm³ of carbon dioxide at 760 mm Hg and 27 °C is taken to 950 mm Hg and 127 °C. Find the new volume.
bullets: Step 1: T₁ = 300 K, T₂ = 400 K.
Step 2: V₂ = P₁V₁T₂ ÷ (T₁P₂).
Check: the pressure rise shrinks the gas and the temperature rise expands it; the net result is a small rise.

visual.alt: Worked table for the combined gas equation

slides.narration: Write both states, with the temperatures in kelvin. Pressure goes up, which shrinks the gas. Temperature goes up, which expands it. Multiply seven hundred and sixty by three hundred by four hundred, and divide by three hundred times nine hundred and fifty. The new volume is three hundred and twenty cubic centimetres.

slides.heading: Quick check: pressure and temperature
slides.body_md: A gas at 300 K, 760 mm Hg and 300 cm³ is compressed to 150 cm³ at 1140 mm Hg. What is the final temperature in kelvin?
slides.narration: Rearrange the combined equation for the second temperature.

slides.heading: Standard temperature and pressure
slides.body_md: Gas volumes change with temperature and pressure, so chemists compare gases at **standard temperature and pressure (STP)**.

visual.alt: Table of the values of standard temperature and pressure

slides.narration: Standard temperature is two hundred and seventy three kelvin, which is zero degrees Celsius. Standard pressure is seven hundred and sixty millimetres of mercury, which is one atmosphere. To reduce a volume to standard conditions, put those values in as the second state of the gas equation.

slides.heading: Worked example 4: reduction to STP
slides.body_md: A gas has volume 800 cm³ at 570 mm Hg and 91 °C. Find its volume at STP.
bullets: Step 1: T₁ = 91 + 273 = 364 K; STP: P₂ = 760 mm Hg, T₂ = 273 K.
Step 2: V₂ = P₁V₁T₂ ÷ (T₁P₂).

visual.alt: Worked table for the reduction to standard temperature and pressure

slides.narration: The first temperature in kelvin is three hundred and sixty four. Substitute the standard values for the second state. The volume at standard temperature and pressure comes to four hundred and fifty cubic centimetres.

slides.heading: Quick check: to STP
slides.body_md: 10 dm³ of a gas at 2280 mm Hg and 27 °C is reduced to STP. Find its volume in dm³.
slides.narration: Change the temperature to kelvin first.

slides.heading: Summary
bullets: Kelvin = Celsius + 273; absolute zero is 0 K or −273 °C.
Charles's law: at constant pressure V ∝ T (kelvin), V₁/T₁ = V₂/T₂.
Extrapolating the V–t line gives zero volume at −273 °C.
Combined equation: P₁V₁/T₁ = P₂V₂/T₂, always with T in kelvin.
STP is 273 K and 760 mm Hg.

visual.alt: Summary table of the gas laws

slides.narration: To recap. Temperatures for gas laws are always in kelvin. Charles law says volume is proportional to kelvin temperature at constant pressure. Extending the graph shows absolute zero. Boyle and Charles combine into one equation, which lets us reduce any gas volume to standard temperature and pressure.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: Convert to **kelvin** before using any gas-law equation with temperature.
State **constant pressure** in Charles's law and **constant temperature** in Boyle's law.
For STP write **273 K and 760 mm Hg**, then substitute in the gas equation.
Show the working: given, formula, substitution, answer with unit.
slides.narration: Exam tips. Change temperatures to kelvin first. Say which quantity is constant in each law. For standard conditions, use two hundred and seventy three kelvin and seven hundred and sixty millimetres of mercury. And always show your working with units.

sections.heading: 1. Behaviour of gases explained by molecular motion
sections.body_md:
The molecules of a gas are **far apart**, move **at random in straight lines** and collide with each other and with the walls of the container. This explains the properties of gases: they have no fixed shape or volume, fill their container, and can be compressed because there is much empty space between molecules.

**Pressure** is the force exerted by the gas on each unit area of the wall. It is caused by the **countless collisions** of molecules with the wall.

| Change | Observation | Explanation |
|---|---|---|
| Gas heated in a closed rigid vessel | Pressure rises | Molecules move faster: harder and more frequent hits on the wall |
| Gas heated under a free piston | Volume increases | Faster molecules push the piston out until the pressure inside again equals the outside pressure |
| Gas compressed at constant temperature | Pressure rises | The same molecules hit a smaller area of wall more often |
| Gas cooled | Pressure or volume falls | Slower molecules hit less hard and less often |

The average speed of the molecules depends on the temperature, not on the pressure.

key_terms.definition_md: The force that gas molecules exert on each unit area of the container wall by colliding with it.

sections.heading: 2. Boyle's law
sections.body_md:
**Statement:** at constant temperature, the volume of a fixed mass of gas is **inversely proportional** to its pressure.

**Derivation of the form:** $V \propto 1/P$, so $V = k/P$, that is $PV = k$ (a constant). For a gas taken from one state to another at the same temperature, $P_1V_1 = P_2V_2$.

**Explanation by molecules:** when the volume is made smaller, the molecules are packed into a smaller space and hit each unit area of wall more often, so the pressure rises.

**Graphs** (fixed mass, constant temperature):
- P against V: a **curve** (rectangular hyperbola) that never meets the axes.
- P against 1/V: a **straight line through the origin**.
- PV against P: a **horizontal straight line**.

Imagined readings: V = 20, 25, 40, 50, 100 cm³ with P = 600, 480, 300, 240, 120 mm Hg give P × V = 12000 each time.

key_terms.definition_md: At constant temperature the volume of a fixed mass of gas is inversely proportional to its pressure.

sections.heading: 3. Charles's law and absolute zero
sections.body_md:
**Statement:** at constant pressure, the volume of a fixed mass of gas is **directly proportional to its absolute temperature (in kelvin)**.

$V \propto T$, so $V/T = k$ and $\dfrac{V_1}{T_1} = \dfrac{V_2}{T_2}$.

Older books state it in the Celsius form: for each degree Celsius rise (or fall) in temperature, the volume changes by $1/273$ of its volume at 0 °C, that is $V_t = V_0\left(1 + \dfrac{t}{273}\right)$. Both forms give the same results.

**Graphs:**
- V against Celsius temperature: a straight line that does **not** pass through the origin. If it is extended backwards (**extrapolated**), it meets the temperature axis at **−273 °C**, where the volume would be **zero**.
- V against kelvin temperature: a straight line **through the origin**.

**Absolute zero** is $0$ K ($−273$ °C), the lowest possible temperature. Real gases condense to liquids (and then solids) before reaching it, so the zero-volume point is obtained only by extrapolation. Imagined readings: V = 125, 150, 175, 200 cm³ at −23, 27, 77, 127 °C.

sections.body_md:
**Conversion:** $T\text{ (K)} = t\text{ (°C)} + 273$ and $t = T - 273$. A kelvin degree and a Celsius degree are the same size.

| Celsius | Kelvin |
|---|---|
| −273 °C | 0 K (absolute zero) |
| 0 °C | 273 K (ice melts) |
| 27 °C | 300 K |
| 100 °C | 373 K (water boils) |

**STP (standard temperature and pressure):** **273 K** (0 °C) and **760 mm Hg** (1 atmosphere). Gas volumes are compared at STP because they depend on temperature and pressure. (Textbooks that use the value −273.15 °C give 273.15 K; ICSE Class IX uses 273 K.)

**Temperatures must be in kelvin in every gas-law calculation.** Using degrees Celsius gives wrong answers.

sections.heading: 5. The gas equation and reduction to STP
sections.body_md:
**Derivation:** take a fixed mass of gas from $(P_1, V_1, T_1)$ to $(P_2, V_2, T_2)$ in two steps.
1. Change the pressure from $P_1$ to $P_2$ at constant $T_1$ (Boyle): the volume becomes $V' = P_1V_1/P_2$.
2. Change the temperature from $T_1$ to $T_2$ at constant $P_2$ (Charles): $V'/T_1 = V_2/T_2$.

Combining: $\dfrac{P_1V_1}{T_1} = \dfrac{P_2V_2}{T_2}$, the **combined gas equation**.

**Reduction to STP:** put $P_2 = 760$ mm Hg and $T_2 = 273$ K, so $V_0 = \dfrac{P_1V_1 \times 273}{T_1 \times 760}$.

**Method for every problem:** (1) list the given values for the two states, (2) change °C to K, (3) use the same units for the two pressures and the two volumes, (4) rearrange, substitute, and give the answer with its unit, (5) check that the direction of change is sensible.

Worked results (imagined data): 300 cm³ at 760 mm Hg and 27 °C becomes 320 cm³ at 950 mm Hg and 127 °C; 800 cm³ at 570 mm Hg and 91 °C becomes 450 cm³ at STP.

key_terms.definition_md: The relation P₁V₁/T₁ = P₂V₂/T₂ for a fixed mass of gas, obtained by combining Boyle’s and Charles’s laws.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Common mistakes**
- Using degrees Celsius instead of **kelvin** in Charles's law or the gas equation.
- Writing Boyle's law without **constant temperature** and **fixed mass**, or Charles's law without **constant pressure**.
- Saying the P–V graph is a straight line. It is a **curve**; the **P against 1/V** graph is the straight line through the origin.
- Mixing units, such as one pressure in mm Hg and the other in atmospheres.
- Forgetting to say that the zero-volume point at −273 °C comes from **extrapolation**.
- Giving STP as 0 K or 100 °C; it is **273 K and 760 mm Hg**.

**How marks are usually awarded**
- 1 mark: a law, a term, a conversion or a standard value.
- 2 marks: a short calculation with the formula, or an explanation using molecules.
- 3 marks: a numerical with working or three-point answer.
- 10-mark structured question: a data table, a graph or apparatus followed by parts such as conversions, a calculation, a law and an explanation.

answer.model_answer_md:

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** 27 + 273 = **300 K**; −33 + 273 = **240 K**.

**(b)** P₁V₁/T₁ = P₂V₂/T₂.

**(c)** V₂ = P₁V₁T₂ ÷ (T₁P₂) = 760 × 20 × 240 ÷ (300 × 380) = **32 dm³**.

**(d)** V = 760 × 20 ÷ 380 = **40 dm³**.

**(e)** The **fall in pressure increases** the volume (20 to 40 dm³); the **fall in temperature decreases** it (40 to 32 dm³).

questions.solution_md: 300 K and 240 K; gas equation; 32 dm³; 40 dm³; pressure fall raises and temperature fall lowers the volume.

(c) The load on A is increased. State the change in the volume of B and explain it using molecules. [3]

(d) The gas has a volume of 450 cm³ at 760 mm Hg. Find its volume when the load raises the pressure to 2280 mm Hg. [2]

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** A: **piston with load**. C: **thermometer**. E: **water bath**.

**(c)** The volume **decreases**. The same molecules are in a **smaller space**, so they strike **each unit area of wall more often**, which balances the greater pressure.

**(d)** V₂ = 760 × 450 ÷ 2280 = **150 cm³**.

**(e)** The volume **increases**.

questions.solution_md: Piston with load, thermometer, water bath; constant temperature; volume falls, more collisions per unit area; 150 cm³; volume increases.

questions.stem_md:
A student working in a hill-station laboratory collects 1000 cm³ of a gas at 27 °C and 684 mm Hg.

(a) State the values of standard temperature and pressure. [2]

(b) Express the laboratory temperature in kelvin. [1]

(c) Calculate the volume of the gas at STP. [3]

(d) The gas at STP is then warmed to 273 °C at constant pressure. Find its volume. [2]

(e) Explain why the volume in (c) is smaller than the volume collected. [2]

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** **273 K** (0 °C) and **760 mm Hg** (1 atmosphere).

**(b)** 27 + 273 = **300 K**.

**(c)** V₀ = 684 × 1000 × 273 ÷ (300 × 760) = **819 cm³**.

**(d)** 819 × 546 ÷ 273 = **1638 cm³**.

**(e)** Two changes act: the pressure at STP is **higher** (760 against 684 mm Hg) and the temperature at STP is **lower** (273 against 300 K). Both **reduce** the volume.

questions.solution_md: 273 K and 760 mm Hg; 300 K; 819 cm³; 1638 cm³; higher pressure and lower temperature both reduce the volume.

questions.stem_md:
The graph shows the pressure of a fixed mass of a gas at different volumes at constant temperature.

(a) Name the law the graph illustrates and use two points to show that the data obey it. [3]

(b) From the graph, read the pressure at 30 cm³ and the volume at 150 mm Hg. [2]

(c) Using the law, calculate the pressure when the volume is reduced to 18 cm³. [2]

(d) Describe the graph obtained by plotting P against 1/V for the same gas. [1]

(e) The experiment is repeated at a higher temperature. State how the position of the curve changes and explain with molecules. [2]

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** **Boyle's law**. At 20 cm³ the pressure is 450 mm Hg, so P × V = 9000; at 45 cm³ it is 200 mm Hg, so P × V = 9000. The products are **equal**.

**(b)** At 30 cm³: **300 mm Hg**; at 150 mm Hg: **60 cm³**.

**(c)** P = 9000 ÷ 18 = **500 mm Hg**.

**(d)** A **straight line through the origin**.

**(e)** The curve lies **higher** (more pressure at each volume), because the molecules move **faster** and hit the walls harder and more often.

questions.solution_md: Boyle's law with equal products; 300 mm Hg and 60 cm³; 500 mm Hg; straight line through the origin; curve moves up.

marking_scheme.step: Faster molecules, harder and more frequent hits
